column6: Je coupe une tomate pour la salade.
column7: I am cutting a tomato for the salad.
column8: It is feminine in French (la tomate), unlike Italian pomodoro, which is masculine.

column6: Il mange une carotte crue.
column7: He is eating a raw carrot.
column8: It is spelled with a double t, unlike Italian carota.

column6: Elle coupe un oignon pour la sauce.
column7: She is cutting an onion for the sauce.
column8: The i is silent: it is pronounced as if spelled ognon.

column6: Je mets de la confiture sur mon pain.
column7: I put jam on my bread.
column8: Means jam or preserves for spreading; often used with the partitive article (de la confiture).

column6: Je mange du jambon avec du pain.
column7: I eat ham with bread.
column8: Without further detail it usually means cooked ham; raw ham is jambon cru.

column6: Je prends un yaourt au petit-déjeuner.
column7: I have a yoghurt for breakfast.
column8: The usual spelling is yaourt, different from English yoghurt.

column6: Je voudrais de la glace à la vanille.
column7: I would like some vanilla ice cream.
column8: It also means ice; context tells the two meanings apart.

column6: Les enfants mangent un biscuit après l'école.
column7: The children eat a biscuit after school.
column8: The final t is silent.

column6: Ma mère prépare une tarte aux pommes.
column7: My mother is making an apple tart.
column8: Means an open tart or pie; it is feminine.

column6: Il faut de la farine pour ce gâteau.
column7: You need flour for this cake.
column8: It is feminine and uncountable, so it takes the partitive article (de la farine).

column6: Je mets de l'huile dans la poêle.
column7: I put oil in the pan.
column8: It is feminine (the h is silent), unlike Italian olio, which is masculine.

column6: Je mets du poivre sur la viande.
column7: I put pepper on the meat.
column8: Not to be confused with poivron, the bell pepper.

column6: Cette fraise est très sucrée.
column7: This strawberry is very sweet.
column8: Strawberry is fraise; raspberry is framboise.

column6: Il mange une banane le matin.
column7: He eats a banana in the morning.
column8: It is feminine; the final e is silent and the n is clearly pronounced.

column6: Je veux un citron pour mon thé.
column7: I want a lemon for my tea.
column8: Means lemon, not the large fruit English calls citron (French cédrat).

column6: Il y a un champignon dans la sauce.
column7: There is a mushroom in the sauce.
column8: The plural takes -s (les champignons); gn is pronounced like ny in canyon.

column6: Il achète une saucisse pour le barbecue.
column7: He is buying a sausage for the barbecue.
column8: The dry sausage sliced cold is called saucisson, not saucisse.

column6: Quelle boisson voulez-vous avec votre repas ?
column7: Which drink would you like with your meal?
column8: It is feminine and covers any drink; the related verb is boire.

column6: Elle pose une assiette sur la table.
column7: She puts a plate on the table.
column8: Means the plate you eat from; the dish or course itself is plat.

column6: Je coupe le pain avec un couteau.
column7: I cut the bread with a knife.
column8: The plural ends in -x: couteaux.

column6: Tu as une fourchette pour les pâtes ?
column7: Do you have a fork for the pasta?
column8: It is feminine; ch is pronounced /ʃ/, like sh in ship.

column6: Je mange la soupe avec une cuillère.
column7: I eat the soup with a spoon.
column8: It is feminine; the variant spelling cuiller also exists.

column6: Il y a une bouteille d'eau dans mon sac.
column7: There is a bottle of water in my bag.
column8: It is feminine; eille is pronounced /ɛj/.

column6: Je voudrais une tasse de café.
column7: I would like a cup of coffee.
column8: Means the cup for hot drinks; a drinking glass is verre.

column6: Elle ferme le rideau le soir.
column7: She closes the curtain in the evening.
column8: The plural ends in -x: rideaux.

column6: Les clés sont dans le tiroir.
column7: The keys are in the drawer.
column8: It is masculine; the ending -oir appears in other object nouns, such as couloir.

column6: Il y a des livres sur l'étagère.
column7: There are some books on the shelf.
column8: Covers both a single shelf and a set of shelves.

column6: Le lait est dans le réfrigérateur.
column7: The milk is in the refrigerator.
column8: In everyday speech it is often shortened to frigo.

column6: Le gâteau est dans le four.
column7: The cake is in the oven.
column8: Means the oven; a microwave is a four à micro-ondes.

column6: Il y a de la vaisselle dans l'évier.
column7: There are dishes in the sink.
column8: Means the kitchen sink; a bathroom basin is a lavabo.

column6: Elle prend un bain dans la baignoire.
column7: She takes a bath in the bathtub.
column8: The gn is pronounced /ɲ/, like ny in canyon.

column6: Mon bureau est au bout du couloir.
column7: My office is at the end of the corridor.
column8: Means the corridor of a home or a building.

column6: Nous gardons le vin dans la cave.
column7: We keep the wine in the cellar.
column8: Means a cellar under a building; a natural cave is a grotte.

column6: Il met la voiture dans le garage.
column7: He puts the car in the garage.
column8: It is masculine; the final g is pronounced /ʒ/.

column6: Notre appartement a une grande pièce.
column7: Our flat has one big room.
column8: Means a room of a home; it can also mean coin or piece.

column6: Le loyer augmente chaque année.
column7: The rent goes up every year.
column8: It is the amount you pay; the verb to rent is louer.

column6: Ce meuble est très lourd.
column7: This piece of furniture is very heavy.
column8: The plural les meubles means furniture in general.

column6: Il y a un coussin sur le canapé.
column7: There is a cushion on the sofa.
column8: Means a decorative or seat cushion; the one for sleeping is an oreiller.

column6: J'ai froid, je prends une couverture.
column7: I am cold, I am taking a blanket.
column8: Besides blanket, it also means the cover of a book.

column6: Je dors avec un oreiller doux.
column7: I sleep with a soft pillow.
column8: The group -eill- is pronounced /ej/.

column6: Ce drap est blanc et propre.
column7: This sheet is white and clean.
column8: The final p is silent; the plural is draps.

column6: L'ascenseur est en panne aujourd'hui.
column7: The lift is out of order today.
column8: It is masculine; you say prendre l'ascenseur to take it.

column6: J'habite dans un immeuble près de la gare.
column7: I live in an apartment building near the station.
column8: Means a building with several flats, not furniture (that is meuble).

column6: Il y a une lampe au plafond.
column7: There is a lamp on the ceiling.
column8: It also means an upper limit, for example on spending.

column6: Je sors la poubelle chaque soir.
column7: I take out the bin every evening.
column8: It is feminine; you say sortir la poubelle for taking out the rubbish.

column6: Il y a du savon près du lavabo.
column7: There is soap next to the basin.
column8: It is masculine; the final n only nasalises the vowel.

column6: Elle prend une serviette dans la salle de bains.
column7: She takes a towel in the bathroom.
column8: Means both a towel and a table napkin; it can also mean a briefcase.

column6: Il passe l'aspirateur dans le salon.
column7: He vacuums the living room.
column8: It is used with the verb passer: passer l'aspirateur.

column6: Il y a une réduction sur les pulls.
column7: There is a discount on the sweaters.
column8: In a shop it means discount; it also means reduction in general.

column6: Vous avez de la monnaie ?
column7: Do you have any change?
column8: Means small change or the change you get back; it also means currency.

column6: Mon portefeuille est dans mon sac.
column7: My wallet is in my bag.
column8: A coin purse is called a porte-monnaie.

column6: Où est le rayon des fruits ?
column7: Where is the fruit section?
column8: Means a department or aisle in a shop; it also means ray of light.

column6: Le caissier me rend la monnaie.
column7: The cashier gives me my change.
column8: The feminine form is la caissière.

column6: Le prix est sur l'étiquette.
column7: The price is on the label.
column8: Means a product label; it also means etiquette.

column6: Je cherche cette veste en taille moyenne.
column7: I am looking for this jacket in a medium size.
column8: Means clothing size; it also means height and waist.

column6: Quelle est votre pointure ?
column7: What is your shoe size?
column8: It is used for shoes and gloves.

column6: Il fait froid, mets ton manteau.
column7: It is cold, put on your coat.
column8: The plural is manteaux.

column6: Cette veste noire est très jolie.
column7: This black jacket is very pretty.
column8: Means a jacket; a waistcoat is a gilet.

column6: Elle porte une jupe bleue.
column7: She is wearing a blue skirt.
column8: The u is pronounced /y/, as in the French word tu.

column6: Ce pull rouge coûte vingt euros.
column7: This red sweater costs twenty euros.
column8: It is short for pull-over; it is pronounced /pyl/, not as in English.

column6: J'ai perdu une chaussette dans la machine.
column7: I lost a sock in the machine.
column8: It is often used in the plural (les chaussettes) because socks come in pairs.

column6: Elle achète un parfum pour sa mère.
column7: She is buying a perfume for her mother.
column8: Means both perfume and the flavour of an ice cream.

column6: Je regarde la vitrine de ce magasin.
column7: I am looking at the window of this shop.
column8: It appears in the expression faire du lèche-vitrines, meaning to go window shopping.

column6: Il pousse le chariot dans le magasin.
column7: He pushes the trolley through the shop.
column8: Means the trolley used in a supermarket or an airport.

column6: Ma commande arrive demain.
column7: My order arrives tomorrow.
column8: Means an order for goods or a meal; it also means a control of a machine.

column6: La boulangerie ouvre à sept heures.
column7: The bakery opens at seven o'clock.
column8: It is the shop; the person who works there is le boulanger.

column6: Je paie la facture d'électricité aujourd'hui.
column7: I am paying the electricity bill today.
column8: It also means a utility bill; the restaurant bill is addition.

column6: Ce bijou est un cadeau de ma mère.
column7: This jewel is a gift from my mother.
column8: The plural ends in -x: bijoux.

column6: J'ai oublié mon passeport à la maison.
column7: I forgot my passport at home.
column8: The final t is not pronounced. It is masculine: le passeport.

column6: Nous passons la douane sans problème.
column7: We go through customs without any problem.
column8: You say passer la douane for "to go through customs". It is feminine.

column6: Mon bagage est très lourd.
column7: My luggage is very heavy.
column8: It is often used in the plural, les bagages, like Italian "bagagli".

column6: Le départ du train est à huit heures.
column7: The train's departure is at eight o'clock.
column8: It is masculine, while Italian "partenza" is feminine. Its opposite is l'arrivée.

column6: Nous attendons son arrivée à la gare.
column7: We are waiting for his arrival at the station.
column8: It is feminine, while Italian "arrivo" is masculine.

column6: Le train a deux heures de retard.
column7: The train is two hours late.
column8: You say être en retard for "to be late". It is masculine.

column6: J'ai fait une réservation pour ce soir.
column7: I made a booking for tonight.
column8: You say faire une réservation for "to make a booking". It is feminine.

column6: La frontière est à dix kilomètres.
column7: The border is ten kilometres away.
column8: It is feminine. It refers to the line between two countries.

column6: La visite dure environ une heure.
column7: The visit lasts about an hour.
column8: It is used for a visit to a place or to a person. It is feminine.

column6: Mon village est très calme.
column7: My village is very quiet.
column8: It is masculine: le village. It is smaller than a ville.

column6: La route est fermée à cause de la neige.
column7: The road is closed because of the snow.
column8: It means the road between towns. It is feminine.

column6: Le pont est très ancien.
column7: The bridge is very old.
column8: Faire le pont also means taking an extra day off between a holiday and the weekend.

column6: L'horaire du bus change demain.
column7: The bus timetable changes tomorrow.
column8: It is used for transport and work schedules. It is masculine.

column6: Notre séjour à Nice dure une semaine.
column7: Our stay in Nice lasts one week.
column8: Le séjour can also mean the living room of a home.

column6: Ils habitent à la campagne.
column7: They live in the countryside.
column8: It is the opposite of la ville. You say à la campagne for "in the countryside".

column6: Mon salaire arrive à la fin du mois.
column7: My salary arrives at the end of the month.
column8: It is masculine. It is used for any pay received from an employer.

column6: Il travaille dans une usine de voitures.
column7: He works in a car factory.
column8: It is feminine. It refers to a place where goods are made.

column6: Cette entreprise cherche un nouveau directeur.
column7: This company is looking for a new manager.
column8: It mainly means "company". It is feminine.

column6: Le directeur est dans son bureau.
column7: The manager is in his office.
column8: The feminine form is la directrice.

column6: J'ai un entretien demain matin.
column7: I have an interview tomorrow morning.
column8: It means a job interview and also the maintenance of a thing.

column6: Il a signé son contrat hier.
column7: He signed his contract yesterday.
column8: The final t is not pronounced. It is masculine.

column6: Elle fait un stage dans une banque.
column7: She is doing an internship at a bank.
column8: It means an internship or a short course. The person doing it is le stagiaire.

column6: Le chômage a baissé cette année.
column7: Unemployment fell this year.
column8: Être au chômage means to be unemployed.

column6: L'ouvrier répare le toit.
column7: The worker is repairing the roof.
column8: The feminine is ouvrière. It refers to a manual worker.

column6: Je cherche le dossier du client.
column7: I am looking for the client's file.
column8: It means a folder of papers or a computer folder. It is masculine.

column6: Mon père est à la retraite.
column7: My father is retired.
column8: Être à la retraite means to be retired. It is feminine.

column6: Cette formation dure trois mois.
column7: This training lasts three months.
column8: It often means a professional training course. It is feminine.

column6: J'aime l'histoire de France.
column7: I like the history of France.
column8: It means both history as a subject and a story: une histoire drôle.

column6: Ce peintre est très célèbre.
column7: This painter is very famous.
column8: It refers to someone who paints. The verb is peindre.

column6: Ce tableau est dans le musée.
column7: This painting is in the museum.
column8: The plural takes -x: «les tableaux», like «bateau» and «gâteau».

column6: Je lis un roman policier.
column7: I am reading a detective novel.
column8: The person who writes novels is le romancier.

column6: L'auteur signe ses livres demain.
column7: The author signs his books tomorrow.
column8: In auteur the letters au are read as o.

column6: Elle apprend un poème par cœur.
column7: She is learning a poem by heart.
column8: It is masculine. The person who writes poems is le poète.

column6: Cette exposition ouvre samedi.
column7: This exhibition opens on Saturday.
column8: It mainly means an art or photo exhibition. It is feminine.

column6: Nous visitons un château.
column7: We are visiting a castle.
column8: The plural is les châteaux. It can also mean a historic mansion.

column6: La cathédrale est au centre-ville.
column7: The cathedral is in the city centre.
column8: In French it is spelled with th, unlike Italian "cattedrale".

column6: C'est une tradition de famille.
column7: It is a family tradition.
column8: It is feminine and looks like Italian "tradizione".

column6: Ce château date du douzième siècle.
column7: This castle dates from the twelfth century.
column8: It is masculine: le siècle.

column6: Le spectacle commence à vingt heures.
column7: The show starts at eight p.m.
column8: It means a stage show such as theatre, dance or circus. It is masculine.

column6: La bibliothèque ferme à six heures.
column7: The library closes at six o'clock.
column8: It means a place to borrow books, not a bookshop, which is a librairie.

column6: Il y a une statue devant l'église.
column7: There is a statue in front of the church.
column8: It is feminine, like Italian "statua".

column6: Nous faisons une randonnée dimanche.
column7: We are going on a hike on Sunday.
column8: You say faire une randonnée for "to go on a hike".

column6: J'aime la montagne en hiver.
column7: I like the mountains in winter.
column8: It is feminine, like Italian "montagna".

column6: La mer est froide en mars.
column7: The sea is cold in March.
column8: It is feminine, while Italian "mare" is masculine. It sounds the same as mère, "mother".

column6: Nous marchons dans la forêt.
column7: We are walking in the forest.
column8: It is feminine. It has a circumflex on the e.

column6: Le lac est très profond.
column7: The lake is very deep.
column8: The final c is pronounced. It is masculine.

column6: Nous dormons sous la tente.
column7: We sleep in the tent.
column8: It means a camping tent. It is feminine.

column6: Nous restons dans un camping.
column7: We are staying at a campsite.
column8: In French le camping means the place itself, the campsite.

column6: On fait un pique-nique au parc.
column7: We are having a picnic in the park.
column8: It is written with a hyphen. The plural is les pique-niques.

column6: L'enfant joue avec un ballon.
column7: The child is playing with a ball.
column8: It is not related to the Italian word "ballo".

column6: La soirée était très agréable.
column7: The evening was very pleasant.
column8: It means the evening as an event or a party. The time of day itself is le soir, masculine.

column6: La sortie est à droite.
column7: The exit is on the right.
column8: It means both an exit from a place and an outing, like une sortie au cinéma.

column6: Mon loisir préféré est la lecture.
column7: My favourite hobby is reading.
column8: It is often used in the plural: les loisirs.

column6: Mon père adore le bricolage.
column7: My father loves DIY.
column8: It means small repair or building jobs at home. The verb is bricoler.

column6: J'ai un rhume depuis deux jours.
column7: I have had a cold for two days.
column8: You say avoir un rhume for "to have a cold".

column6: Ma toux ne passe pas.
column7: My cough is not going away.
column8: The final x is not pronounced. It is feminine.

column6: J'ai une douleur au dos.
column7: I have a pain in my back.
column8: It is feminine, while Italian "dolore" is masculine.

column6: Le médecin écrit une ordonnance.
column7: The doctor is writing a prescription.
column8: In this sense it means a doctor's prescription. It is feminine.

column6: Je prends un médicament le soir.
column7: I take a medicine in the evening.
column8: The plural is les médicaments. It is masculine.

column6: L'infirmière change le pansement.
column7: The nurse changes the dressing.
column8: The masculine form is l'infirmier.

column6: Cette maladie est très rare.
column7: This illness is very rare.
column8: It is feminine. It has the same root as malade.

column6: Sa blessure au genou est grave.
column7: His knee injury is serious.
column8: It means a wound or an injury, including a sports injury.

column6: Elle a une allergie au lait.
column7: She has an allergy to milk.
column8: You say être allergique à for "to be allergic to".

column6: Il met un pansement sur son doigt.
column7: He puts a bandage on his finger.
column8: It means a plaster or a dressing. It is masculine.

column6: Le vaccin protège contre cette maladie.
column7: The vaccine protects against this illness.
column8: The matching verb is vacciner.

column6: Il suit un régime sans sucre.
column7: He is on a sugar-free diet.
column8: It also means a political regime.

column6: J'ai besoin de sommeil.
column7: I need sleep.
column8: You say avoir sommeil for "to be sleepy".

column6: Nous sommes retournés à Paris.
column7: We went back to Paris.
column8: Meaning 'to go back', it takes être in the passé composé; with an object ('retourner une crêpe') it takes avoir.

column6: Elle est remontée dans le train.
column7: She got back on the train.
column8: Used without an object it takes être in the passé composé; with a direct object it takes avoir.

column6: Elle a nettoyé la cuisine hier.
column7: She cleaned the kitchen yesterday.
column8: Verbs in -oyer change y to i before a silent e: je nettoie, but nous nettoyons.

column6: Tu as rangé ta chambre ce matin.
column7: You tidied your room this morning.
column8: Before a and o it adds an e to keep the soft g sound: nous rangeons.

column6: Nous avons décoré le sapin ensemble.
column7: We decorated the Christmas tree together.
column8: It is a regular -er verb that takes a direct object: décorer une pièce.

column6: Ils ont organisé une belle fête.
column7: They organized a lovely party.
column8: It is a regular -er verb and takes avoir in the passé composé.

column6: Il a accepté notre invitation.
column7: He accepted our invitation.
column8: It takes a direct object or de + infinitive: accepter de venir.

column6: Vous avez refusé cette offre.
column7: You turned down this offer.
column8: It takes a direct object or de + infinitive: refuser de partir.

column6: Elle a proposé un nouveau plan.
column7: She suggested a new plan.
column8: The pattern is proposer à qqn de + infinitive: je te propose de venir.

column6: Nous avons essayé ce restaurant.
column7: We tried this restaurant.
column8: The y may stay or become i (j'essaie, j'essaye); before an infinitive it takes essayer de.

column6: Tu as ajouté trop de sel.
column7: You added too much salt.
column8: It takes a direct object and à: ajouter du sel à la soupe.

column6: Il a cassé mon verre.
column7: He broke my glass.
column8: It is transitive: casser qqch; the form se casser means 'to break (by itself)'.

column6: Elle a réussi son examen.
column7: She passed her exam.
column8: With an exam it is réussir un examen, with no preposition; with an infinitive it is réussir à faire.

column6: Ils ont grandi à la campagne.
column7: They grew up in the countryside.
column8: It is a regular -ir verb (grandissons); it is intransitive and takes avoir in the passé composé.

column6: Vous avez rempli le formulaire.
column7: You filled in the form.
column8: It is a regular -ir verb (remplissons); remplir un formulaire means 'to fill in a form'.

column6: Il a rendu ce pull hier.
column7: He returned this sweater yesterday.
column8: It is a regular -re verb; with an adjective it means 'to make' (rendre heureux).

column6: Nous avons applaudi les musiciens.
column7: We applauded the musicians.
column8: It is a regular -ir verb used directly with its object: applaudir un artiste.

column6: Elle a réfléchi toute la nuit.
column7: She thought it over all night.
column8: The pattern is réfléchir à qqch; it is a regular -ir verb (réfléchissons).

column6: Je les laisse devant ma porte.
column7: I leave them in front of my door.
column8: Followed by an infinitive it means 'to let': laisser entrer; with an object it means 'to leave (something)'.

column6: Nous la gardons pour ce soir.
column7: We are keeping it for tonight.
column8: It means 'to keep' and also 'to babysit': garder des enfants.

column6: Ils le partagent avec leurs amis.
column7: They share it with their friends.
column8: Before a and o it adds an e: nous partageons.

column6: Je le présente à ma famille.
column7: I am introducing him to my family.
column8: To introduce a person you say présenter qqn à qqn.

column6: Elle les quitte à midi.
column7: She leaves them at noon.
column8: It always takes a direct object: quitter la maison, with no preposition.

column6: Nous la remarquons tout de suite.
column7: We notice it right away.
column8: It means 'to notice' and is a regular -er verb.

column6: Je les remercie pour ce cadeau.
column7: I thank them for this gift.
column8: The pattern is remercier qqn de or pour qqch.

column6: On le retrouve devant ce café.
column7: We are meeting him in front of this cafe.
column8: It means 'to find again' something lost and also 'to meet' someone at a set place.

column6: Nous la traversons à pied.
column7: We cross it on foot.
column8: It is directly transitive: traverser la rue, with no preposition.

column6: Elle les vérifie chaque matin.
column7: She checks them every morning.
column8: It takes a direct object: vérifier un horaire; it is a regular -er verb.

column6: Mon père la répare ce soir.
column7: My father is repairing it tonight.
column8: It means 'to repair' an object and is a regular -er verb.

column6: Je le goûte avant de servir.
column7: I taste it before serving.
column8: It means 'to taste' (also goûter à qqch) and as a verb also 'to have an afternoon snack'.

column6: Nous les nourrissons chaque matin.
column7: We feed them every morning.
column8: It is a regular -ir verb (nourrissons) used for people and animals.

column6: Elle ne les punit jamais.
column7: She never punishes them.
column8: It is a regular -ir verb (punissons); the pattern is punir qqn de or pour qqch.

column6: Mon grand-père raconte une belle histoire.
column7: My grandfather tells a beautiful story.
column8: It is used for stories and events: raconter une histoire à qqn.

column6: Le bus tourne à droite ici.
column7: The bus turns right here.
column8: It is a regular -er verb; it also means 'to shoot' a film.

column6: Nous changeons de train à Lyon.
column7: We change trains in Lyon.
column8: Before a and o it adds an e; it is changer de + noun with no article.

column6: Ma fille dessine un chat.
column7: My daughter is drawing a cat.
column8: It means 'to draw' and is a regular -er verb.

column6: Ils décident de manger dehors.
column7: They decide to eat outside.
column8: The pattern is décider de + infinitive: il décide de partir.

column6: Nous allons rêver de vacances.
column7: We are going to dream of holidays.
column8: The pattern is rêver de qqch or rêver de + infinitive.

column6: Tu vas confondre ces deux mots.
column7: You are going to confuse these two words.
column8: It is a regular -re verb (confondons); the pattern is confondre A avec B.

column6: L'avion va atterrir à midi.
column7: The plane is going to land at noon.
column8: It is a regular -ir verb (atterrissons) and takes avoir in the passé composé.

column6: Nous allons vieillir ensemble.
column7: We are going to grow old together.
column8: It is a regular -ir verb (vieillissons); it takes avoir in the passé composé.

column6: Il a grossi pendant l'hiver.
column7: He gained weight during the winter.
column8: It means 'to gain weight'; it is a regular -ir verb with avoir in the passé composé.

column6: Elle a maigri en deux mois.
column7: She lost weight in two months.
column8: It means 'to lose weight'; it is a regular -ir verb with avoir in the passé composé.

column6: Le chien a obéi tout de suite.
column7: The dog obeyed right away.
column8: It takes à: obéir à qqn; it is a regular -ir verb.

column6: Le conducteur a ralenti devant l'école.
column7: The driver slowed down in front of the school.
column8: It is a regular -ir verb that can be used without an object: ralentir devant l'école.

column6: Nous avons défendu notre projet.
column7: We defended our project.
column8: It means 'to defend' but also 'to forbid' (défendre à qqn de faire).

column6: Elle a guéri très vite.
column7: She recovered very quickly.
column8: It is a regular -ir verb; intransitive it means 'to recover' (avoir), transitive 'to cure someone'.

column6: Nous nous levons à sept heures.
column7: We get up at seven o'clock.
column8: In the present the e becomes è before a silent syllable: je me lève, but nous nous levons.

column6: Les enfants se couchent à neuf heures.
column7: The children go to bed at nine o'clock.
column8: Se coucher means 'to go to bed'; coucher qqn means 'to put someone to bed'.

column6: Je me réveille à six heures.
column7: I wake up at six o'clock.
column8: Se réveiller means 'to wake up'; réveiller qqn means 'to wake someone up'.

column6: Nous nous promenons au parc.
column7: We go for a walk in the park.
column8: Se promener means 'to go for a walk'; in the present it takes è: je me promène.

column6: Vous vous habillez toujours en noir.
column7: You always dress in black.
column8: S'habiller means 'to get dressed'; in the passé composé it takes être: je me suis habillé.

column6: Nous nous dépêchons ce matin.
column7: We are hurrying this morning.
column8: Se dépêcher means 'to hurry' and is often followed by de + infinitive.

column6: Tu te reposes après le travail.
column7: You rest after work.
column8: Se reposer means 'to rest'; in the passé composé it takes être.

column6: Nous nous installons au salon.
column7: We settle in the living room.
column8: S'installer means 'to settle in'; installer qqch means 'to install'.

column6: Nous nous amusons beaucoup ici.
column7: We have a lot of fun here.
column8: S'amuser means 'to have fun'; amuser qqn means 'to entertain someone'.

column6: Nous nous arrêtons devant le café.
column7: We stop in front of the cafe.
column8: S'arrêter means 'to stop (oneself)'; arrêter qqch means 'to stop' or 'to quit' something.

column6: Nous nous brossons les dents.
column7: We brush our teeth.
column8: With body parts it uses the article: se brosser les dents.

column6: Vous vous excusez trop souvent.
column7: You apologize too often.
column8: S'excuser means 'to apologize'; the pattern is s'excuser de or pour qqch.

column6: Nous nous inquiétons pour toi.
column7: We are worried about you.
column8: S'inquiéter means 'to worry'; in the singular present the é becomes è: je m'inquiète.

column6: Elle se maquille avant la fête.
column7: She puts on make-up before the party.
column8: Se maquiller means 'to put on make-up'; the reflexive pronoun agrees with the subject.

column6: Je ne peux pas croire cette histoire.
column7: I cannot believe this story.
column8: It is irregular (je crois, nous croyons); the patterns are croire à qqch and croire en qqn.

column6: Elle veut vivre à Lyon.
column7: She wants to live in Lyon.
column8: It is irregular (je vis, nous vivons); the past participle is vécu.

column6: Vous devez suivre cette route.
column7: You must follow this road.
column8: It is irregular (je suis, nous suivons); je suis is identical to the form of être.

column6: Tu peux tenir mon sac.
column7: You can hold my bag.
column8: It is irregular (je tiens, nous tenons); the past participle is tenu.

column6: J'aime courir le matin.
column7: I like running in the morning.
column8: It is irregular (je cours, nous courons); the past participle is couru.

column6: Nous aimons rire ensemble.
column7: We like laughing together.
column8: It is irregular (je ris, nous rions); the past participle ri never changes.

column6: Ce film va plaire aux enfants.
column7: This film is going to please the children.
column8: It is irregular with the participle plu; the person is an indirect object: plaire à qqn.

column6: Je veux offrir des fleurs.
column7: I want to give flowers as a gift.
column8: In the present it is conjugated like an -er verb (j'offre); the past participle is offert.

column6: Mon frère sait conduire une moto.
column7: My brother knows how to ride a motorbike.
column8: It is irregular (je conduis, nous conduisons); the past participle is conduit.

column6: Cette plante va mourir sans eau.
column7: This plant is going to die without water.
column8: It is irregular; in the passé composé it takes être: il est mort.

column6: Le bébé doit naître en mai.
column7: The baby is due to be born in May.
column8: It is irregular; in the passé composé it takes être: elle est née.

column6: Elle veut devenir médecin.
column7: She wants to become a doctor.
column8: It is irregular; in the passé composé it takes être: il est devenu.

column6: Tu peux revenir demain soir.
column7: You can come back tomorrow evening.
column8: It is irregular; in the passé composé it takes être: il est revenu.

column6: Il espère obtenir son visa.
column7: He hopes to get his visa.
column8: It is irregular; in the passé composé it takes avoir: il a obtenu.

column6: Nous voulons découvrir cette ville.
column7: We want to discover this city.
column8: It is irregular; the past participle is découvert.

column6: Il ne veut plus souffrir.
column7: He does not want to suffer any more.
column8: It is irregular; the past participle is souffert.

column6: Elle aime sourire aux clients.
column7: She likes to smile at customers.
column8: It is irregular; the pattern is sourire à qqn and the past participle is souri.

column6: Il faut éteindre la lumière.
column7: You have to turn off the light.
column8: It is irregular (j'éteins, nous éteignons); the past participle is éteint.

column6: Il aime peindre des paysages.
column7: He likes to paint landscapes.
column8: It is irregular (je peins, nous peignons); the past participle is peint.

column6: Peux-tu traduire cette phrase ?
column7: Can you translate this sentence?
column8: It is irregular (je traduis, nous traduisons); the past participle is traduit.

column6: Ils vont construire une école.
column7: They are going to build a school.
column8: It is irregular (je construis, nous construisons); the past participle is construit.

column6: Cette carte va vous permettre de voyager.
column7: This card is going to allow you to travel.
column8: The pattern is permettre à qqn de faire; the past participle is permis.

column6: Tu dois promettre de revenir.
column7: You must promise to come back.
column8: The pattern is promettre à qqn de faire; the past participle is promis.

column6: Je peux reconnaître sa voix.
column7: I can recognize her voice.
column8: It is irregular, with î before t (il reconnaît); the past participle is reconnu.

column6: Ma chambre est très propre.
column7: My room is very clean.
column8: After the noun it means clean; before the noun it means own (ma propre chambre).

column6: Ce village est assez pauvre.
column7: This village is quite poor.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine. Before the noun it can mean unfortunate, pitiable (mon pauvre ami).

column6: Mon oncle est très riche.
column7: My uncle is very rich.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; the plural is riches.

column6: Ce film est trop court.
column7: This film is too short.
column8: Feminine courte. It describes things and duration; for a person's height French uses petit.

column6: Cette montagne est très haute.
column7: This mountain is very high.
column8: The h is aspirated: no liaison or elision (le haut). Feminine haute. For people French uses grand.

column6: Les prix sont bas ici.
column7: Prices are low here.
column8: Feminine basse; the masculine plural stays bas. For a person's height French uses petit, not bas.

column6: Cette rue est très large.
column7: This street is very wide.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine. It can also describe loose-fitting clothes.

column6: Ce couloir est trop étroit.
column7: This hallway is too narrow.
column8: Feminine étroite. It is the opposite of large.

column6: Mon pull est très doux.
column7: My sweater is very soft.
column8: Feminine douce. It describes fabrics, weather and gentle people; for sugary sweetness French uses sucré.

column6: Ce fromage est trop dur.
column7: This cheese is too hard.
column8: Feminine dure. It can also describe a tough task or a hard time.

column6: Ce pain est trop sec.
column7: This bread is too dry.
column8: The feminine is irregular: sèche.

column6: Mes chaussures sont toutes mouillées.
column7: My shoes are all wet.
column8: Past participle of mouiller used as an adjective; it agrees: mouillé, mouillée, mouillés, mouillées.

column6: Il a un gros chat.
column7: He has a big cat.
column8: Irregular feminine: grosse. It is usually placed before the noun.

column6: Ce livre est très mince.
column7: This book is very thin.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine. Said of a person it means slim.

column6: Cette idée est vraiment folle.
column7: This idea is really crazy.
column8: Irregular feminine: folle (plural fous, folles).

column6: Ce film est vraiment drôle.
column7: This film is really funny.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine. Before a noun it can mean strange (une drôle d'idée).

column6: Mon patron est très sérieux.
column7: My boss is very serious.
column8: Feminine sérieuse. It also describes someone reliable and hard-working.

column6: Ma fille est un peu timide.
column7: My daughter is a bit shy.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine.

column6: Mon frère est un peu paresseux.
column7: My brother is a bit lazy.
column8: Feminine paresseuse.

column6: Cette infirmière est très courageuse.
column7: This nurse is very brave.
column8: Feminine courageuse. The related noun is le courage.

column6: Cet enfant est très poli.
column7: This child is very polite.
column8: Feminine polie. Careful: poli does not mean clean (that is propre).

column6: Le ciel est gris aujourd'hui.
column7: The sky is grey today.
column8: Feminine grise; the masculine plural stays gris.

column6: Elle porte une robe rose.
column7: She is wearing a pink dress.
column8: As a colour adjective it agrees normally (des robes roses). It is also the word for the flower.

column6: J'aime ce sac violet.
column7: I like this purple bag.
column8: Feminine violette; plural violets, violettes.

column6: Mon voisin est très sympathique.
column7: My neighbour is very nice.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine. It means likeable, not sympathetic in the sense of feeling pity.

column6: Ce restaurant est très agréable.
column7: This restaurant is very pleasant.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine.

column6: Cette route est très dangereuse.
column7: This road is very dangerous.
column8: Feminine dangereuse. The related noun is le danger.

column6: Ma mère est très inquiète.
column7: My mother is very worried.
column8: Irregular feminine: inquiète.

column6: Elle vit seule à Lyon.
column7: She lives alone in Lyon.
column8: After the verb it means alone; before a noun it means only (le seul problème).

column6: Cette histoire est vraie.
column7: This story is true.
column8: Feminine vraie. It is the opposite of faux.

column6: Cette réponse est fausse.
column7: This answer is wrong.
column8: Irregular feminine: fausse. It can also mean fake (un faux billet).

column6: La mer est très calme.
column7: The sea is very calm.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine.

column6: Ce quartier est trop bruyant.
column7: This neighbourhood is too noisy.
column8: Feminine bruyante. The related noun is le bruit.

column6: Ce village est très tranquille.
column7: This village is very peaceful.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine; it is spelled with two l.

column6: Ce chanteur est très célèbre.
column7: This singer is very famous.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine.

column6: Ce bruit est vraiment étrange.
column7: This noise is really strange.
column8: Same form for masculine and feminine. Do not confuse it with étranger, which means foreign.

column6: Cette église est très ancienne.
column7: This church is very old.
column8: Feminine ancienne. After the noun it means ancient; before the noun it means former (mon ancien patron).

column6: Le prochain train part bientôt.
column7: The next train leaves soon.
column8: Feminine prochaine. It can stand before or after the noun: le prochain train, la semaine prochaine.

column6: Le dernier métro est parti.
column7: The last metro has left.
column8: Feminine dernière. Before the noun it means final in a series; after a time noun it means previous (l'année dernière).

column6: Ce gâteau est vraiment délicieux.
column7: This cake is really delicious.
column8: Feminine délicieuse.

column6: Il est fatigué, pourtant il travaille.
column7: He is tired, yet he is working.
column8: An adverb that introduces a contrast with what was just said.

column6: Nous avons enfin des vacances !
column7: We finally have holidays!
column8: It marks the end of a wait (enfin!) and can also close a list.

column6: Nous allons ensuite prendre le train.
column7: Then we are going to take the train.
column8: It says what comes next in time; it is written as one word.

column6: Je vais d'abord prendre une douche.
column7: I am going to take a shower first.
column8: It contains an apostrophe. It is often paired with ensuite and enfin to order actions.

column6: Elle a surtout mal au dos.
column7: She has back pain especially.
column8: It is written as one word; the final t is silent.

column6: Nous sommes presque arrivés.
column7: We have almost arrived.
column8: As an adverb it does not elide: «presque arrivé»; the elision appears only in «presqu'île».

column6: Le musée est à environ dix minutes.
column7: The museum is about ten minutes away.
column8: It goes before a number. The plural les environs is a noun meaning surroundings.

column6: Ce film est plutôt long.
column7: This film is rather long.
column8: It is written with a circumflex on the o.

column6: Je n'ai pas dormi longtemps.
column7: I did not sleep for long.
column8: It is written as one word; the final s is silent.

column6: Je ne rentre pas tard ce soir.
column7: I am not coming home late this evening.
column8: It is the opposite of tôt. Plus tard means later.

column6: Je ne me lève pas tôt le dimanche.
column7: I do not get up early on Sundays.
column8: It is the opposite of tard. It has a circumflex and the final t is silent.

column6: La gare n'est pas très loin d'ici.
column7: The station is not very far from here.
column8: It is the opposite of près. With a complement it becomes loin de.

column6: Mon père est quelquefois très fatigué.
column7: My father is sometimes very tired.
column8: It is written as one word and is a synonym of parfois.

column6: Cette valise est assez lourde.
column7: This suitcase is quite heavy.
column8: Before a noun it takes de: assez de.

column6: Ce café est trop chaud.
column7: This coffee is too hot.
column8: Before a noun it takes de: trop de. The final p is silent.

column6: J'ai des livres partout.
column7: I have books everywhere.
column8: It is written as one word; the final t is silent.

column6: Les enfants sont dehors.
column7: The children are outside.
column8: It is the opposite of dedans. En dehors de means apart from or outside of.

column6: Nous allons dîner ailleurs ce soir.
column7: We are going to have dinner elsewhere tonight.
column8: D'ailleurs means besides or by the way.

column6: Nous allons dormir pendant le voyage.
column7: We are going to sleep during the trip.
column8: It is used with an event or a duration (pendant deux heures).

column6: Je suis ici depuis deux ans.
column7: I have been here for two years.
column8: For an action still going on, French uses the present tense (je suis ici depuis...).

column6: Il va rentrer vers huit heures.
column7: He is going to come home around eight o'clock.
column8: With a time it means around; with a place it shows direction.

column6: Le café est entre la banque et la poste.
column7: The cafe is between the bank and the post office.
column8: It sounds the same as the form il entre of the verb entrer.

column6: Je suis contre cette idée.
column7: I am against this idea.
column8: It is the opposite of pour. It expresses opposition and physical contact (contre le mur).

column6: Selon Marie, le magasin est fermé.
column7: According to Marie, the shop is closed.
column8: It goes with a person or a source; selon moi means in my opinion.

column6: Il est content malgré la pluie.
column7: He is happy despite the rain.
column8: It is written with an acute accent on the final e.

column6: Il est malade, donc il reste ici.
column7: He is ill, so he is staying here.
column8: It is pronounced /dɔ̃k/ at the start of a sentence or before a vowel; before a consonant the «c» is often silent.

column6: Je reste ici, car j'ai froid.
column7: I am staying here because I am cold.
column8: It is more common in writing. Un car is also a coach, but that is a different word.

column6: Il est grand comme son père.
column7: He is as tall as his father.
column8: It can also mean since when it starts a sentence.

column6: Mange vite, sinon tu vas avoir faim.
column7: Eat quickly, otherwise you are going to be hungry.
column8: It is written as one word.

column6: Je vais lui téléphoner demain.
column7: I am going to call him tomorrow.
column8: An indirect object pronoun, the same for masculine and feminine (téléphoner à quelqu'un).

column6: Je vais leur donner un cadeau.
column7: I am going to give them a present.
column8: As a pronoun it is invariable and never takes an s; do not confuse it with the possessive leur, leurs.

column6: Chacun a son téléphone.
column7: Everyone has their own phone.
column8: Feminine chacune. It takes a singular verb.

column6: Quelqu'un est dans la cuisine.
column7: Someone is in the kitchen.
column8: It contains an apostrophe and is masculine singular. Before an adjective it takes de: quelqu'un de gentil.

column6: Je n'ai rien dans mon sac.
column7: I have nothing in my bag.
column8: With a verb it works with ne ... rien. It can stand alone as an answer (Rien!).

column6: Tout est prêt pour la fête.
column7: Everything is ready for the party.
column8: As a pronoun it means everything; the final t is silent.

column6: Plusieurs de mes amis sont malades.
column7: Several of my friends are ill.
column8: It is always plural and has the same form for both genders.

column6: J'habite dans un quartier calme.
column7: I live in a quiet neighbourhood.
column8: It means a district of a town; for «quarter» you say «quart».

column6: La météo annonce de la pluie.
column7: The forecast announces rain.
column8: It is feminine and everyday; «le temps» is the weather itself.

column6: Notre voiture est en panne.
column7: Our car has broken down.
column8: It is used in the phrase «en panne»: a breakdown of a car or a machine.

column6: Il y a eu un accident hier.
column7: There was an accident yesterday.
column8: It is masculine; used for road accidents and accidents in general.

column6: J'emprunte un livre à la bibliothèque.
column7: I borrow a book from the library.
column8: You say «emprunter … à quelqu'un»; the one who lends «prête».

column6: Nous prêtons nos vélos aux voisins.
column7: We lend our bikes to the neighbours.
column8: It is the opposite of «emprunter»: the person giving uses «prêter».

column6: Nous dépensons trop pendant les soldes.
column7: We spend too much during the sales.
column8: It is mainly used for money; for time you say «passer du temps».

column6: J'annule ma réservation pour ce soir.
column7: I cancel my booking for tonight.
column8: It is regular; written with two n.

column6: Pour le dessert, il prend une glace.
column7: For dessert, he has an ice cream.
column8: Masculine; the final t is silent. Do not confuse it with désert, the desert.

column6: Il mange un sandwich au fromage.
column7: He eats a cheese sandwich.
column8: Masculine; the plural is written sandwichs or sandwiches.

column6: Il achète un croissant à la boulangerie.
column7: He buys a croissant at the bakery.
column8: Masculine; the final t is silent.

column6: C'est un rendez-vous très important.
column7: It is a very important appointment.
column8: The feminine is importante and the plural importants.

column6: Ce gâteau est vraiment délicieux.
column7: This cake is really delicious.
column8: It strengthens an adjective or verb: vraiment bon, j'aime vraiment ça.

column6: Il y a seulement deux places libres.
column7: There are only two free seats.
column8: A synonym of uniquement; it goes next to the word it limits.

column6: Je vais me laver les mains avant le repas.
column7: I am going to wash my hands before the meal.
column8: Before an infinitive use avant de: avant de manger. It is the opposite of après.

column6: Après le dîner, j'ai envie de marcher.
column7: After dinner, I feel like walking.
column8: Before a verb use après avoir or après être + participle: après avoir mangé.

column6: Il pleut, alors nous allons rester à la maison.
column7: It is raining, so we are going to stay home.
column8: As a conjunction it introduces a consequence; it can also be an adverb (then, at that time).

column6: La cerise qui tombe de l'arbre est mûre.
column7: The cherry that falls from the tree is ripe.
column8: Feminine; it looks quite different from the Italian word ciliegia.

column6: Je voudrais une poire bien mûre.
column7: I would like a nicely ripe pear.
column8: Feminine; in the familiar expression une bonne poire it means a gullible person.

column6: Le serveur qui s'occupe de notre table parle trois langues.
column7: The waiter who looks after our table speaks three languages.
column8: The feminine is «serveuse». To call a waiter you say «Monsieur» or «S'il vous plaît».

column6: La sauce que j'ai préparée accompagne parfaitement le poisson.
column7: The sauce I made goes perfectly with the fish.
column8: It covers sauces and gravies. «Sauce tomate» is tomato sauce.

column6: Notre vol à destination de Lisbonne a duré deux heures.
column7: Our flight to Lisbon lasted two hours.
column8: It also means "theft": the context makes the meaning clear.

column6: Mon collègue m'a remplacé pendant mon absence.
column7: My colleague replaced me during my absence.
column8: Same form for both genders (le/la collègue).

column6: Cette université accueille quarante mille étudiants chaque année.
column7: This university welcomes forty thousand students every year.
column8: In France the université is distinct from the "grandes écoles".

column6: Ce jouet est fabriqué en bois recyclé.
column7: This toy is made from recycled wood.
column8: It is the object one plays with, unlike jeu (the game).

column6: Le train va bientôt partir.
column7: The train is going to leave soon.
column8: Written with a circumflex; À bientôt means see you soon.

column6: Cet été, nous irons jusque dans les Alpes.
column7: This summer, we will go as far as the Alps.
column8: Before a vowel it becomes jusqu'. It is often used with dans, sur, chez, ici.

column6: Nous dînerons d'abord, puis nous irons au cinéma.
column7: We will have dinner first, then we will go to the cinema.
column8: It links successive actions. In speech, et puis adds a further remark.

column6: Je pense que ce village est le plus beau.
column7: I think this village is the most beautiful.
column8: It introduces noun clauses and the second term of comparisons. Before a vowel it becomes qu'.
